title: Development
subject: economics
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 Social Science (087) syllabus: this chapter is fully in the board examination (Economics: 20 marks). There is no map item from this chapter. Data tables follow the current NCERT book (World Development Report 2019, HDR 2019, state data 2017–19). NCERT exercises that need personal surveys or long data tables are left out.

blocks.title: One dam, two stories
blocks.body:
A big dam brings electricity and irrigation to towns and farms far away. For an industrialist it is development. But for an adivasi family whose village and forest will be drowned by the dam, it means losing home and livelihood.

So what is development, and for whom? This chapter asks how different people see development, how we compare countries and states, why income alone is not enough, and why development must be sustainable.

blocks.title: Development as freedom
blocks.body:
Indian economist **Amartya Sen** won the **Nobel Prize in Economics in 1998**. He argued that development is not only about rising income, but about expanding the real **freedoms and capabilities** of people: to be healthy, educated, free and able to take part in society.

His ideas helped shape the **Human Development Index** used by the United Nations Development Programme, which compares countries on health, education and income, not income alone.
blocks.future: This chapter leads to careers in economics, development studies, public policy, statistics and environmental management.

blocks.question: Why can the same project be development for one person and harmful for another?
options: Because people have different goals, and what helps one group can hurt another
Because only the government decides what development means
blocks.explanation: Different people can have different as well as conflicting notions of development.

sections.title: Different goals, income and other goals

blocks.title: What development promises to different people
blocks.body:
**Different people, different goals:** people seek things that are most important for them, that can fulfil their aspirations or desires. Different persons can have **different developmental goals**, and these goals can even be **conflicting**: what may be development for one may not be development for another, and may even be destructive for the other.
- For example, an industrialist may want more dams to get more electricity, but this may submerge the land and disrupt the lives of people who are displaced, such as **tribals**.

**Income and other goals:** what people desire are **regular work, better wages and a decent price** for their crops or products. In other words, they want **more income**. But besides seeking more income, people also seek things like **equal treatment, freedom, security and respect** of others. They resent discrimination.
- In some cases, non-material things may be more important than more income or more consumption, because material goods are not all that you need to live. For example, if women are engaged in paid work, their dignity in the household and society increases; but there must also be **respect** for women and a **safe and secure environment** for them to take up jobs or run a business.
- Money, or material things that one can buy with it, is one factor on which our life depends. But the quality of our life also depends on **non-material things**, which are often not easy to measure but mean a lot to our lives. So, for development, people look at a **mix of goals**.

**National development:** if individuals seek different goals, their notion of national development is also likely to be different. Even the idea of what constitutes national development may differ. We need to think about whether there may be a **better way of doing things**, and whether a particular way of development is **fair and just** for most people.

blocks.title: Developmental goals of different categories of persons (NCERT)
blocks.body:
| Category of person | Developmental goals / aspirations |
|---|---|
| Landless rural labourers | more days of work and better wages; local school for children; no social discrimination |
| Prosperous farmers from Punjab | higher family income through higher support prices and hardworking, cheap labourers; settling children abroad |
| Farmers who depend only on rain | assured irrigation, so that crops do not fail |
| A rural woman from a land-owning family | freedom, security, respect and equal treatment |
| Urban unemployed youth | a job with good pay |
| A boy from a rich urban family | good education and a chance to study abroad |
| A girl from a rich urban family | as much freedom as her brother to decide what she wants to do |
| An adivasi from the Narmada valley | no displacement by a big dam; protection of land, forests and livelihood |

blocks.title: Average income and its limits
blocks.body:
**How to compare countries:** for comparing countries, their **income** is considered one of the most important attributes. Countries with higher income are more developed than others with less income. But the total income of a country does not tell us what an average person is likely to earn, as populations differ. So we compare the **average income**:
- **Average income = total income of the country ÷ total population.** It is also called **per capita income**.
- The **World Bank**, in its **World Development Report**, uses per capita income as the criterion for classifying countries. In the **World Development Report 2019** (as given in NCERT), countries with a per capita income of **US$ 12,056 per annum and above in 2017** are called **rich countries**, and those with **US$ 955 or less** are called **low-income countries**. **India** comes in the category of **low middle income countries** because its per capita income in 2017 was just **US$ 1,820** per annum. The rich countries, excluding countries of the Middle East and certain other small countries, are generally called **developed countries**.

**Limitation of averages:** while averages are useful for comparison, they **hide disparities**. Imagine two countries, each with an average income of Rs 10,000. In country A, all five citizens earn close to Rs 10,000; in country B, one citizen earns Rs 48,000 and four earn Rs 500 each. Both have the same average, but country A is more equitable: people are neither very rich nor extremely poor. In country B, most people are poor.

**Income and other criteria:** is income enough? Compare three states (NCERT table below). **Haryana** has the highest per capita income and **Bihar** the lowest. But **Kerala**, with a lower per capita income than Haryana, has a much **lower infant mortality rate** and higher literacy and attendance.
- **Infant mortality rate (IMR):** the number of children that die **before the age of one year** as a proportion of **1000 live children** born in that particular year.
- **Literacy rate:** the proportion of literate population in the **7 years and above** age group.
- **Net attendance ratio:** the total number of children of age group **14 and 15 years** attending school as a percentage of the total number of children in the same age group.

**Public facilities:** money in your pocket cannot buy all the goods and services you need to live well. Income by itself is not an adequate indicator of the material goods and services that citizens are able to use. Money cannot buy a **pollution-free environment** or ensure that you get **unadulterated medicines**, unless you can afford to shift to a community that already has all these. Money may also not be able to protect you from **infectious diseases**, unless the whole community takes preventive steps.
- Many important things are best provided **collectively**: it is cheaper to have collective security for the whole locality than for each house to pay for its own; schools, health centres and other facilities work only when the government and community provide them.
- **Kerala** has a low infant mortality rate because it has adequate provision of **basic health and educational facilities**. In some states, the **Public Distribution System (PDS)** functions well, so the health and nutritional status of people there is likely to be better.

blocks.title: The Human Development Report and sustainable development
blocks.body:
**Human Development Report:** once we realise that even though income is important, it is not an adequate criterion, we look for other criteria. The **Human Development Report** published by the **UNDP (United Nations Development Programme)** compares countries based on the **educational levels** of the people, their **health status** and **per capita income**.
- **Life expectancy at birth** denotes, as the name suggests, the average expected length of life of a person at the time of birth.
- **Gross enrolment ratio** for three levels means the enrolment ratio for primary school, secondary school and higher education beyond secondary school.
- **Per capita income** in the HDR is calculated in **dollars** for all countries so that it can be compared, and in a way that every dollar buys the same amount of goods and services in any country (**purchasing power parity**).
- In the Human Development Report 2019 (as in NCERT), **Sri Lanka** (rank **71**) was far ahead of **India** (rank **129**) in human development, even though Sri Lanka is a much smaller country. India's neighbours Bangladesh, Nepal, Myanmar and Pakistan ranked below or near India.

**Sustainability of development:** development must not come at the cost of future generations. Scientists have been warning that the present type and levels of development are **not sustainable**.
- **Groundwater:** recent evidence suggests that the groundwater in the country is under serious threat of **overuse**. Groundwater is an example of a **renewable resource**: it is replenished by nature, as in the case of crops and plants. But even these resources may be overused: in the case of groundwater, if we use more than what is being replenished by rain, we would be overusing it.
- **Non-renewable resources** are those which will get exhausted after years of use. We have a fixed stock on earth which cannot be replenished. We do discover new resources, which increases the available stock, but over time even these will be exhausted. **Crude oil** is an example: if the world continues to extract it at the present rate, the reserves will last only for a limited number of years. India has to import much of its oil, which makes it vulnerable.
- **Environmental degradation** is not confined to a nation or state. Issues like this are **no longer regional or national**; our future is linked together. **Sustainability of development** is a comparatively new area of knowledge in which scientists, economists, philosophers and other social scientists are working together.
- In general, the question of development or progress is perennial. At all times, as members of society and as individuals, we need to ask **where we want to go, what we wish to become and what our goals are**.

blocks.question: The Human Development Report compares countries on:
options: educational levels, health status and per capita income
blocks.explanation: It is published by the UNDP.
option_feedback: That is the World Bank's main criterion.

blocks.question: Which is a renewable resource that can still be overused?
blocks.explanation: If we use more groundwater than rain replenishes, we overuse it.

blocks.title: Memory tricks
blocks.body:
- **Per capita income = Total income ÷ Population.**
- **World Bank (WDR 2019): Rich ≥ US$ 12,056; Low ≤ US$ 955; India = US$ 1,820 (low middle).**
- **UNDP HDI = "HEI"**: Health (life expectancy), Education (literacy, enrolment), Income (per capita, in PPP dollars).
- **IMR = deaths before age 1 per 1000 live births; Literacy = age 7+; Attendance = age 14–15.**
- **Kerala vs Haryana: "Kerala Keeps Kids alive"**: lower income, but IMR 7 against 30.
- **Renewable = Replenished (groundwater); Non-renewable = Not replenished (crude oil).**

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
1. Saying everyone has the same development goals: goals are **different and can conflict**.
2. Thinking total income is the best comparison: we use **average (per capita) income** because populations differ.
3. Forgetting that averages **hide disparities**.
4. Saying Kerala has the highest per capita income: **Haryana** has the highest of the three; Kerala does best on health and education.
5. Mixing up the World Bank and UNDP: the World Bank uses **per capita income**; the UNDP uses **health, education and income**.
6. Calling groundwater non-renewable: it is **renewable**, but can be overused.

blocks.title: Try this in class
blocks.body: Give five students imaginary incomes (for example Rs 500, 500, 500, 500 and 48,000). Ask the class to find the average and then ask: does the average describe these five people well? Repeat with five nearly equal incomes with the same average.

blocks.title: Think and explain
blocks.body: Write down three development goals for yourself and three for your locality. Which of them are about income, and which are about non-material things like safety, respect or clean air?

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
'Per capita income is not a useful criterion at all.' Do you agree? Answer in about 120 words.

**Model answer:** I do not fully agree. Per capita income is useful: dividing total income by population lets us compare countries of different sizes, and the World Bank uses it to classify countries as rich, middle-income or low-income. But it has limitations. Being an average, it hides disparities: two countries with the same average may have very different distributions of income. It also ignores non-material goals and public facilities. Kerala has a lower per capita income than Haryana, yet its infant mortality rate is much lower and its literacy and school attendance are higher, because of good health and educational facilities. So per capita income should be used along with other indicators, such as those in the UNDP's Human Development Index.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Different people have different, and sometimes conflicting, development goals; people want income and also equality, freedom, security and respect.
- Countries are compared by per capita (average) income; the World Bank classifies countries this way, with India in the low middle income group.
- Averages hide disparities, and income does not show access to public facilities.
- Kerala, with a lower per capita income than Haryana, does far better on infant mortality, literacy and attendance.
- The UNDP's Human Development Report compares countries on education, health and income; Sri Lanka ranks well above India.
- Development must be sustainable: groundwater is overused and crude oil is running out.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- The 2025-26 sample paper asked about the limitation of per capita income (it gives a basic idea of well-being but hides income inequality; answer C) and the utility of public services (health, education, sanitation and clean water, infrastructure) for well-being (3 marks).
- 3/5-mark favourites: different goals, limitations of per capita income, Kerala and Haryana comparison, World Bank vs UNDP criteria, sustainability.
- Learn the definitions of IMR, literacy rate and net attendance ratio exactly.

blocks.back: The total income of a country divided by its total population; also called average income.

blocks.back: The number of children that die before the age of one year as a proportion of 1000 live children born in that year.

blocks.front: On what does the UNDP's Human Development Report compare countries?
blocks.back: Educational levels, health status and per capita income.
Development that meets present needs without using up resources or damaging the environment for future generations.
